title: Category Trees That Can Change: Designing Marketplace Taxonomies
basis: Reconstructed on 2026-11-12 from the published index.md (paragraph for paragraph, in its own order) and spec.md (accepted 2026-10-21), which it replaces. Intent outcome, the three acceptance criteria AC-1 to AC-3, the thesis and the role are copied unchanged from the chapter's entry in journal-spec.json. Five units are new in this pass and do not exist in the published text: p48 (lead-in to the trade-offs table), p49 (lead-in to the vertical-differences table), p45 (lead-in to the 'Everything else that moved' table), p66 (the conclusion's synthesis and callback); p03's roadmap was extended to name every section.

know: What a category controls, the structural choices (strict tree, polyhierarchy, facets; classification versus navigation; one tree or many) and mappings to external taxonomies.
What a taxonomy release contains and how splits, merges, moves and retirements are run as migrations.
believe: A category is a schema key, not a label, so a taxonomy change is a schema migration.
can_do: Diagnose the Category Straitjacket in their own platform.
Plan a category split covering listings, saved searches, URLs, partner codes, models and analytics.

audience.who: Experienced architects and engineering leaders working on listing marketplaces: chief and enterprise architects of marketplace groups, principal and staff engineers, search, data and ML leads, platform-engineering leads, product and engineering directors of classifieds, real-estate, automotive, jobs and recommerce marketplaces, and technology leaders integrating acquired marketplaces.
already_knows: What an API, a database, an event stream, a search engine and Kubernetes are.
How to make and defend an architecture decision.

From earlier chapters: a leaf category, a paid bump, a saved search, the listing aggregate that records a category ID and the taxonomy version it was classified under, required attributes enforced on create and revise, Veldmark and its brands, cast and Common Ground program.
does_not_know: Marketplace economics: liquidity, network effects, multi-homing.
Search and ML vocabulary: learning to rank, percolation, hybrid retrieval.
Regulatory detail: DSA statements of reasons, DAC7, P2B.
Vertical specifics: VINs, property and vehicle feed standards.
The attribute dictionary and category schemas, which attribute-schemas defines after this chapter; here an attribute schema is only the set of fields a category requires or permits.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a requested category split, the reader lists what the release must carry and what must be migrated besides the tree.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Product wants the generic 'Bikes' leaf split into city, e-bikes, cargo and kids' bikes next month in four countries. Using only this chapter: what does the release contain, and what else has to move?
acceptance_criteria.expected: A new canonical tree version with stable IDs, a mapping from every retired node, the attribute diff and effective dates. Existing listings are reclassified by rules, a model above a confidence threshold and seller confirmation, gated by an audit; saved searches are rewritten to preserve results, retired URLs redirected, partner codes accepted for a window with warnings, search mappings and models updated, and analytics given a mapping view instead of rewritten history. Country views keep local labels and navigation.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the opening alone (the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading) can predict the chapter's sections.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the callouts and the paragraphs before the first heading: what will this chapter discuss, in what order, and with what kind of evidence?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Veldmark's six weeks for a new leaf; what a category controls; four structural choices; the taxonomy as versioned reference data and its service; mapping to external taxonomies; migrations and the runbook; category prediction; the bikes split in practice and the harmonization of four trees; trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's view. Evidence: public company engineering sources, external taxonomy standards and the fictional Veldmark.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reverse outline of the chapter, written without the spec, lists the same controlling ideas in the same order as the post spec's sections and paragraphs.
Given a platform where adding a category needs a code release, the reader names the cause in the chapter's terms and the change that removes it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In your marketplace, adding a category takes six weeks: engineers edit fee and moderation rules, the search schema and SEO tables, and analysts fix dashboards. Using only this chapter: what is the underlying cause, and what would you change so the next category takes days?
acceptance_criteria.expected: The Category Straitjacket: the category is treated as content while it behaves as a schema key, so its IDs (or names and slugs) are hard-coded across systems and country trees diverge. Fix: one canonical classification tree with stable, meaningless IDs, rules that read category properties from a taxonomy service, navigation, labels and slugs kept separate, and changes shipped as versioned releases that consumers pin; measure lead time for a new category.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader explains why a merge maps deterministically while a split needs reclassification, and describes the large-model-labeler pattern without attributing an accuracy figure to it.
acceptance_criteria.probe: Using only this chapter: why is merging two categories easier than splitting one, and how did Mercari reclassify its items after renewing its category structure? How accurate was it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: In a merge every listing has one destination; in a split each listing must be decided among the children, so a single from-to mapping can name only a default. Mercari had a large language model label a sample of several million items, choosing among generated candidate categories, and propagated the labels with a k-nearest-neighbor classifier over embeddings that include the original category; it published no accuracy figure.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given a proposed distinction, the reader decides between a new leaf and an attribute value by the chapter's rule and names the change class.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A category manager wants a new leaf 'Electric cargo bikes' under Bikes because e-cargo bikes keep landing in E-bikes. Using only this chapter: should it be a leaf or an attribute, and what kind of change is it?
acceptance_criteria.expected: An attribute (electric assist on Cargo bikes) unless the distinction changes a contract such as schema, fee, policy or ad segment; Veldmark ruled that cargo wins over electric. Adding an optional attribute is an additive change, decided by taxonomy team review with a two-day lead time.

thesis.question: How do you design a category taxonomy that serves sellers, buyers, search, ads and analytics, and evolve it without breaking everything?
thesis.claim: The category is a schema key, not a label: it selects the attributes, validation, fees, moderation, facets, ranking and ad targeting of every listing in it, so a marketplace needs one canonical classification tree with stable IDs and leaf-only listing, with navigation trees, country views, labels, slugs and external mappings derived from it, published by an owned taxonomy service as versioned releases that carry a mapping from every retired node, an attribute diff and effective dates; splits and merges are then run as migrations of listings, saved searches, URLs, partner codes, models and analytics.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that categories are editorial content edited in an admin tool, that each country keeps its own tree, and that a split is a reorganization product managers decide and engineering ships in a coordinated release.
thesis.so_what: A Chief Architect who accepts this removes category IDs from code, runs the taxonomy as a product with an owner, classifies changes by blast radius (cosmetic the same day, additive in two days, structural in two to four weeks) and tracks lead time for a new category: Veldmark's fell from six weeks to two days, and its bikes split reclassified 410,000 listings behind a 95% audit gate and rewrote about 1.3 million saved searches.
thesis.how_why: Category IDs end up in fee rules, moderation rules, search mappings, SEO tables, dashboards and partner feeds, so an edit made like content ripples like a schema change, and the tree hardens into the Category Straitjacket while the 'Other' leaf grows. Separating classification from navigation lets Poland keep bikes under its 'Sport i hobby' browse node while models and ad segments address one e-bike leaf in four countries.

supporting_claims.claim: The category is a schema key, not a label: it selects the attribute schema, fees, moderation, facets, ranking, ad targeting and landing pages, so editing it like content spreads its IDs through code and hardens the tree into the Category Straitjacket.

Classification is one canonical, strict, leaf-only tree with stable IDs; navigation trees, country views, labels and slugs are derived from it and can change without touching listings, and a leaf exists only where it changes a contract.

An owned taxonomy service publishes the tree as versioned reference data: immutable releases, each carrying a mapping from every retired node, an attribute diff and effective dates, which consumers pin and load from a cached snapshot.

External taxonomies (Google, schema.org, vehicle and occupation classifications) are mapping targets held as versioned tables, never the internal model, because they change on someone else's schedule.

A taxonomy change is a migration: merges map deterministically, splits need reclassification by rules, a model and sellers behind an audit gate, and saved searches, URLs, attributes, partner codes, models and analytics each need their own step.
Run as a product with an owner, changes classified by blast radius, regular releases and fitness metrics, the taxonomy becomes changeable: at Veldmark a new leaf fell from six weeks to two days.

role.contribution: Turns the category ID the aggregate holds into a governed, versioned tree and a migration practice, and gives the attribute chapter the key its schemas bind to.

flow.rationale: The scene states the problem (six weeks for a new leaf) and the body solves it in the order each idea needs the one before. What a category controls comes first because the leaf rule and the release artifacts are defined by the contracts a category selects. The structural choices come next because releases version the canonical tree they define. Releases precede external mappings, which are versioned tables in the same service. Prediction follows, because the migrations after it reclassify split listings with its model; placed after migrations, the runbook would use a model the reader had not met. Migrations come last in the method because they are what a release carries and they use everything before. The bikes split then applies the whole method with numbers. The closing sections widen from Veldmark's case to the reader's platform in a fixed order: trade-offs say when the defaults reverse, vertical differences say how that shifts by vertical, failure modes show what happens when the design is ignored, governance prevents those failures, and the questions turn all of it into a review. Told the other way round, the bikes split would use mappings, tiers and versions before they were defined, and governance would argue for a release process the reader had not yet seen.

hook.content: What is a category? A product manager says 'where the listing goes'; the systems say it decides which fields the insertion form shows and requires, the insertion fee, the moderation rules and models, the facets, the ranking model, the ad targeting and the landing pages.

bridge.from_reader_world: Every architect has seen categories renamed, rearranged and copied in an admin tool as if they were editorial content.
bridge.to_topic: Because they behave like schema, those edits ripple into validation, pricing, search, URLs, saved searches and dashboards, and the tree hardens into the Category Straitjacket; the aggregate's category ID and taxonomy version therefore need a designed tree and release process behind them.

thesis_statement.text: The category is a schema key, not a label: keep one canonical classification tree with stable IDs and leaf-only listing, derive navigation, country views, labels and external mappings from it, ship changes as versioned releases with a mapping, an attribute diff and effective dates, and run splits and merges as migrations of everything that points at a category.
thesis_statement.placement: KEY POINTS callout (all three bullets) and the bolded last sentence of p01.

roadmap.placement: IN THIS CHAPTER callout and paragraph p03, which names the sections in order.

promises.promise: Start at Veldmark, where a new leaf takes six weeks.
Set out what a category controls.
Show the structural choices that separate classification from navigation and countries.
Release the tree as versioned reference data and map it to external taxonomies.
Run splits and merges as migrations, with category prediction to reclassify listings.
Follow Veldmark's bikes split through the whole method.
Close with the trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and the Chief Architect's governance, with questions for a design review.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A product manager calls a category 'where the listing goes', but the systems use it to decide the form, the required fields, fees, moderation, facets, ranking, ad targeting and landing pages, so it is the platform's most widely shared key and the one most often treated as content.

evidence.what: The two answers: 'where the listing goes' against the list of what the systems decide from the category.
evidence.shows: The same field is content to one audience and a key to many systems.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because categories look like content but behave like schema, edits made in an admin tool ripple into validation, pricing, search, URLs, saved searches and dashboards, and after a decade the tree hardens into the Category Straitjacket beside a growing 'Other' bucket.

advances_thesis.how: Names the failure pattern the chapter removes and its cause.

transition_in.carries_over: The category's double nature: content to people, key to systems.
transition_in.introduces: What that double nature does over time: the Category Straitjacket.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The category is the first governed subdomain the listing references and the one that selects the contract for the rest; to escape the Category Straitjacket this chapter designs the tree the aggregate took as given, naming its sections in order (the Veldmark scene, what a category controls, structural choices, versioned releases, external mappings, category prediction, splits and merges as migrations, the bikes split that starts harmonizing four trees, then trade-offs, vertical differences, failure modes and governance) and its evidence (public eBay, Amazon, Google, Shopify and Mercari documentation and the fictional Veldmark), before attribute-schemas designs the schemas a category selects.

evidence.what: The chapter's sections in order and the two kinds of evidence.
evidence.shows: Lets a reader of the opening predict the chapter.

advances_thesis.how: Places the chapter in Part II and announces the design that answers the straitjacket.

transition_in.carries_over: The Category Straitjacket, and the category ID and taxonomy version that listing-aggregate recorded and took as given.
transition_in.introduces: The design this chapter gives the tree behind them, section by section.

sections.heading: Setting the Scene at Veldmark: Six Weeks for a New Leaf
sections.controlling_idea: At Veldmark a request to split one generic bike leaf exposes why a new category takes six weeks, and the group wants the next one to take two days.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the Category Straitjacket at work in one concrete request, with the numbers the later sections resolve.

transition_in.carries_over: The Category Straitjacket described in general.
transition_in.introduces: One marketplace where it costs six weeks per category.

flow.rationale: The request, then why it always takes six weeks, then the data the split must move, then the target and the people who will design it. The six weeks must be explained before the target of two days means anything.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In September 2027 Veldmark's product chief asks for Tradeyard's generic bike leaf to be split into city bikes, e-bikes, cargo bikes and kids' bikes, because buyers cannot filter e-bikes and the group's ad unit cannot target them.

evidence.what: Noor Hassan's request; e-bikes a large share of supply and a larger share of value; no filter for battery capacity or motor position; cargo and kids' bikes in the same leaf as city bikes; an untargetable e-bike retail-media campaign (ads sold to manufacturers).
evidence.source: Fictional Veldmark; scenario ledger, categories-and-taxonomies line
evidence.shows: A category request has buyer, seller and revenue consequences at once.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A new category takes six weeks because each of Tradeyard's four country trees gives it a different ID and the change must be copied by hand into fee and moderation rules, search schemas, SEO tables, dashboards and seller feeds.

evidence.what: Four country trees: 1,420 leaves (NL), 1,380 (BE), 980 (PL), 760 (PT).
evidence.shows: The same category exists four times with four IDs.

evidence.what: The six steps: admin tool per country; fee and moderation rules keyed on IDs in PHP configuration; Solr and Elasticsearch schemas and reindexing; hand-made SEO landing pages; dashboards filtering by category name; professional feeds that map by name.
evidence.shows: Each step is a place where the category ID was treated as content and copied.

transition_in.carries_over: The request for four new leaves.
transition_in.introduces: Why the answer has always been six weeks.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The split must divide bike data spread across 19 country-specific leaves holding about 640,000 live listings, of which about 410,000 sit in generic leaves that need reclassifying and about 230,000 map one to one.

evidence.what: 19 leaves; about 640,000 live listings (NL 380,000, BE 120,000, PL 95,000, PT 45,000); about 410,000 in generic leaves, the rest mapping one to one.
evidence.shows: The size of the migration, not of the tree change.

transition_in.carries_over: The four trees and their separate IDs.
transition_in.introduces: How much listing data the split touches.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The Group Chief Architect wants the next request to take two days, so the bikes split becomes the first migration of the new group taxonomy service, designed with search, data and Poland's general manager, who requires Poland's tree to stay recognizably Polish.

evidence.what: Two-day target set by Common Ground; taxonomy and attribute service live October 2027 with Tradeyard first; split live Monday 1 November 2027; Tomasz Wiśniewski, Priya Raman and Katarzyna Nowak join; Katarzyna's condition.
evidence.shows: Frames the chapter's goal as lead time for the next change, and sets up the country-view requirement.

transition_in.carries_over: The bikes split and its size.
transition_in.introduces: The architect's real goal: not bikes, but the next request in two days.

sections.heading: What a Category Controls
sections.controlling_idea: A category taxonomy is load-bearing because a dozen systems key on the category, and public marketplaces confirm that the category selects the contract a listing must meet.

advances_thesis.how: Defines the taxonomy's terms and shows the category as a schema key with public evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: The six places Tradeyard's change has to touch.
transition_in.introduces: The general list of what depends on a category, with owners.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A category taxonomy is a controlled hierarchy of classes with rules hanging off each class (nodes, leaves and paths), and it is load-bearing because eleven kinds of dependency, each owned by another chapter, key on it.

evidence.what: What depends on the category, an example and the owning chapter: attribute schema and validation, insertion form, fees, moderation, facets, ranking, ad targeting, SEO landing pages, saved searches, analytics, legal disclosures.
evidence.shows: The category is a key in eleven systems, so changing it is never local.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: eBay, Amazon and Google each select a listing's required attributes or requirements from its category or product type, so in public practice the category selects the contract the listing must meet.

evidence.what: eBay: 'every eBay listing must be listed in an eBay leaf category', with required, recommended and optional attributes per leaf.
evidence.shows: Leaf-level contracts in a large public marketplace.

evidence.what: Amazon retrieves attribute requirements per product type and marketplace; Google needs the category to apply category-specific requirements.
evidence.source: Amazon SP-API guide, updated 2026; Google Merchant Center Help, n.d.
evidence.shows: The pattern holds across three companies.

evidence.what: Figure 1: a category-shaped key turning a lock that switches on forms, fees, moderation, filters, ads and landing pages.
evidence.shows: The category as a key, not a label.

transition_in.introduces: Public evidence that marketplaces design it this way.

sections.heading: Four Structural Choices
sections.controlling_idea: Four structural decisions shape a taxonomy, and the defaults that serve most marketplaces are a strict leaf-only classification tree, separate navigation and labels, leaves only where a contract changes, and a canonical tree with country views.

advances_thesis.how: Establishes the canonical tree and the derived layers the rest of the design versions and maps.

transition_in.introduces: Therefore the shape of the tree decides which contracts exist and where; four decisions shape it.

flow.rationale: Four decisions, each set out as options and then my default: tree shape, classification versus navigation, breadth and the 'Other' leaf, one tree or many. Tree shape comes first because leaf-only listing is what the later choices assume; localization comes last because country views are built from the three layers.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Because the category selects the contract, four structural decisions shape every taxonomy (tree shape, classification versus navigation, breadth, one tree or many), and each has a default that works for most marketplaces and conditions under which it does not.

A strict tree, a polyhierarchy and faceted classification place items differently, and each fits a different place: a strict leaf-only tree in classification, polyhierarchy in navigation, a shallow tree with facets in real estate and fashion.

evidence.what: Three structures with how each works, strengths, weaknesses and when each is right.
evidence.shows: Polyhierarchy in classification makes schema, fee and policy ambiguous, which is why it belongs in navigation.

transition_in.introduces: The first: tree, polyhierarchy or facets, with definitions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: My default is a strict classification tree with leaf-only listing, because a listing in an interior node escapes the leaf's schema, fees and policies, and the cost of making sellers choose a leaf is why category prediction is part of the design.

transition_in.carries_over: The comparison of the three structures.
transition_in.introduces: The author's choice and its cost.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Amazon documents browse nodes for navigation separately from product types that define attribute schemas, which I read as showing that classifying for schemas and classifying for browsing are different concerns.

evidence.what: New items are placed 'in the appropriate place(s) within the graph' while the product type decides what must be filled in.
evidence.source: Amazon SP-API, browse nodes and item type keywords, updated 2026
evidence.shows: A large marketplace keeps navigation plural and schema selection single; the lesson is labelled as the author's inference.

transition_in.introduces: The second decision: classification is not navigation.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: I separate three layers: a canonical, strict, leaf-only classification tree with stable IDs that changes only through releases; navigation trees per brand and country that change freely; and labels and slugs that are properties of a node, never its identity.

transition_in.carries_over: Schema selection and browsing are different concerns.
transition_in.introduces: The three layers that keep them apart.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: No number of leaves is correct, but two signals show the tree no longer fits the supply, the share of new listings in 'Other' leaves and attribute sparsity inside a leaf, and Veldmark shows both.

evidence.what: Veldmark's 3,900 distinct attribute keys, 41% used on fewer than 0.1% of listings; generic bike leaves with battery fields applying to a third of listings and wheel-size fields applying only to kids' bikes.
evidence.shows: Sparsity is partly a taxonomy symptom.

transition_in.carries_over: The classification tree as one layer.
transition_in.introduces: The third decision: how broad and deep it should be.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A leaf is justified only when it changes a contract (a schema, fee, policy, facet set or ad segment); any other distinction is an attribute value or a navigation grouping.

transition_in.carries_over: Signals that the tree no longer fits.
transition_in.introduces: The rule that decides whether a new leaf is the answer.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A multi-country marketplace chooses between independent country trees, one translated global tree and a canonical tree with country views, which trade local fit against sharing.

evidence.what: Three models with how each works, strengths and weaknesses; country trees are the Copy-Paste Country in reference data, a global tree leaves local categories homeless, a canonical tree needs governance.
evidence.shows: Only the canonical tree with views keeps both shared semantics and local fit.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth decision: one tree or many across countries.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: I recommend a canonical tree with country views, because each country then decides which canonical nodes it enables, what they are called and how they are browsed, while every node, even a country-only one, keeps a canonical ID that models, ads and analytics share.

evidence.what: Figure 2: the canonical classification tree selects schemas and policies; country views, navigation trees and external mappings are derived from it.
evidence.shows: Labels, slugs, browse paths and partner codes change without touching a listing.

transition_in.carries_over: The three models and Katarzyna's condition that Poland stay Polish.
transition_in.introduces: The recommendation that meets it.

sections.heading: The Taxonomy as Versioned Reference Data
sections.controlling_idea: The canonical tree is reference data, so it needs stable IDs, immutable releases that ship their own migration, and consumers that pin versions, delivered by a small service that keeps the taxonomy off the hot path.

advances_thesis.how: Specifies what a release contains and how it reaches consumers.

transition_in.carries_over: A canonical tree with stable IDs that changes only through releases.
transition_in.introduces: What a release is and what treating the tree as reference data requires.

additional_patterns.applies_to: p20 to p24, the four properties

flow.rationale: Define reference data, then its four properties in the order a release is built (identity, snapshot, migration artifacts, consumers), then the service that implements them and why it is cached. The service makes sense only after the reader knows what it publishes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Reference data is data that other data points at to give it meaning, changes rarely and must be identical wherever used, and treating the taxonomy as versioned reference data means four things.
A node's ID never changes and encodes nothing, names and slugs are separate properties, and a node whose meaning changes is retired and replaced rather than edited.

transition_in.introduces: The first: stable, meaningless IDs.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The tree is published as numbered, immutable snapshots, as Shopify's calendar-versioned releases and eBay's per-tree version number show.

evidence.what: Shopify's Standard Product Taxonomy: calendar-versioned releases such as 2024-07, at most one stable release per quarter.
evidence.shows: A public precedent for numbered releases.

evidence.what: eBay's categoryTreeVersion: 'If a new version is detected, call getCategoryTree or getCategorySubTree to fetch the updated categories'.
evidence.shows: Consumers cache a version and compare it.

transition_in.introduces: The second: immutable releases of the whole tree.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every release ships its migration as four artifacts: the new tree, a from-to mapping for every retired node, an attribute diff and effective dates.

evidence.what: Artifact, content and public precedent: eBay category trees and Shopify releases; eBay getExpiredCategories from/to pairs; eBay bulk aspect files of new, modified and removed entities; eBay expectedRequiredByDate.
evidence.shows: Each artifact has a public precedent.

transition_in.introduces: The third: what a release must carry besides the tree.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: eBay's precedents come from its Taxonomy API, and Shopify goes further by publishing mappings between its own versions and to Google's taxonomy, which makes the migration a data product every consumer applies the same way.

evidence.what: eBay Taxonomy API specification v1.1.1; Shopify product-taxonomy integrations, e.g. 2022-02 to 2024-07 and to Google.
evidence.shows: The mapping can be published as data, not left to each consumer.

transition_in.carries_over: The four artifacts and their eBay precedents.
transition_in.introduces: Where those precedents come from and Shopify's further step.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Consumers pin the version they understand, two versions are live during a migration, and the taxonomy service answers for both, as Google does when it translates older taxonomy versions to the latest.

evidence.what: Google accepts categories from older taxonomy versions and translates them.
evidence.shows: The receiving side of version pinning.

transition_in.introduces: The fourth: consumers pin versions.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At Veldmark the group taxonomy and attribute service is a small product with four interfaces: authoring and review, release publication by event, a read API with snapshots, and an embedded client for the hot path.

evidence.what: Interface, consumers and behavior: change requests with impact analysis; TaxonomyReleased event with links to the four artifacts; full snapshots and lookups by ID and version; an in-memory library.
evidence.shows: The four properties become concrete interfaces.

transition_in.carries_over: The four properties a release needs.
transition_in.introduces: The service that provides them at Veldmark.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A snapshot cached in memory and refreshed on each release makes the taxonomy a dependency only of change, whereas calling the service on every insertion makes it a runtime dependency of supply.

transition_in.introduces: Why it matters: what the listing service depends on at runtime.

sections.heading: Mapping to External Taxonomies
sections.controlling_idea: External taxonomies are mapping targets held as versioned tables, never the internal model, because they change on someone else's schedule.

advances_thesis.how: Places external taxonomies among the derived layers, with cases of external change.

transition_in.introduces: Taxonomies the marketplace must fit but does not own.

flow.rationale: The rule and the six external taxonomies first, then three cases of external change (Google, vehicles, jobs), then the mapping tables that follow from them. The tables answer the problem the cases raise.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A marketplace must emit categories to and ingest them from taxonomies it does not own, and the rule I use is that external taxonomies are mapping targets, never the internal model.

evidence.what: Google product taxonomy, schema.org, Shopify, GS1 GPC, vehicle taxonomies and occupation taxonomies: what each is, how marketplaces use it and a caution for each.
evidence.shows: Each was built for another purpose or changes on its own schedule.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Google added vehicle-listing structured-data documentation in 2023 and removed it in 2025, so a portal that had shaped its vehicle model on it would have reshaped it twice in two years.

evidence.what: Added October 2023, phase-out notices June 2025, removed September 2025 because these types 'are no longer shown in Google Search results'.
evidence.source: Google Search Central, vehicle listing structured data changelog, 2025
evidence.shows: External structures change under you.

transition_in.carries_over: The rule that external taxonomies are targets.
transition_in.introduces: The first of two cases of external change.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Vehicle taxonomies change with the market, so in automotive the tree beneath 'Cars' is a licensed or curated taxonomy the marketplace maps onto, and its changes are migrations like any other.

evidence.what: Auto Trader UK's taxonomy of vehicle types, makes, models, generations and derivatives; release notes of model splits that 'will impact derivatives'.
evidence.shows: Vehicle taxonomies split and change like category trees.

transition_in.introduces: The second case: vehicle taxonomies.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For jobs, a marketplace usually keeps a shallow internal tree for browsing and fees and maps listings to occupation codes such as ESCO as an enrichment, because a job title is not reliably classifiable by the employer.

evidence.what: ESCO v1.2.1 lists 3,039 occupations and 13,939 skills in 28 languages.
evidence.shows: The scale of the external classification a jobs marketplace maps onto.

transition_in.carries_over: External taxonomies in goods and vehicles.
transition_in.introduces: A different use of mapping in jobs: enrichment rather than publishing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Mappings live in the taxonomy service as versioned tables typed exact, broader or narrower, and inbound mappings are owned by ingestion but stored here so a release can update them in the same change.

transition_in.carries_over: External taxonomies that change on their own schedule.
transition_in.introduces: Where and how the mappings are kept.

sections.heading: Category Prediction
sections.controlling_idea: Category prediction serves both insertion and migration, public evidence for it is product-level, and four design rules make it safe.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the model that leaf-only listing and split reclassification both rely on.

transition_in.carries_over: Releases and mappings that say where each node goes.
transition_in.introduces: A model that decides where each listing goes, needed at insertion and in the migrations that follow.

flow.rationale: Definition and why it matters twice, then the limited public evidence, then the rules I draw from it, labelled as recommendations because the evidence is thin. It comes before migrations because their reclassification step runs this model; placed after them, the reader would meet the model in the runbook before it was explained.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Category prediction suggests or assigns a listing's category from its content, and it matters at insertion, where the leaf decides everything that follows, and in migrations, where it reclassifies existing listings.
Public evidence for category prediction is product-level, from eBay's 2023 announcement and a 2025 trade-press report on Kleinanzeigen, with no first-party engineering description.

evidence.what: eBay's 'magical listing' drafts a listing from a photo, including 'detailed category/sub-category'.
evidence.shows: Category suggestion ships in a large marketplace.

evidence.what: Kleinanzeigen suggests title, description and category from a photo across most categories, excluding vehicles and intangibles, and sellers accept fully, partly or not at all.
evidence.shows: Suggestion, not silent assignment, and exclusions where input is complex.

transition_in.introduces: What public marketplaces show of it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four design rules follow, as my recommendations: suggest the top three and let the seller choose, make the model taxonomy-version-aware, measure acceptance and correction, and treat category manipulation as a fraud signal.

evidence.what: Mercari's 2024 attribute-extraction work passing attribute keys at request time (its candidate-category method is described in the next section).
evidence.shows: Candidates can be passed as input so a model survives a new release.

transition_in.introduces: The rules I draw, labelled as recommendations.

sections.heading: Category Migrations: Splits, Merges, Moves and Retirements
sections.controlling_idea: Every taxonomy change other than a label change is a migration; merges are deterministic, splits need reclassification at scale, and a seven-step runbook covers what teams forget.

advances_thesis.how: Defines migrations, their effects on each consumer, the reclassification pattern and the runbook.

transition_in.carries_over: A release's from-to mapping and a prediction model.
transition_in.introduces: What happens to everything that points at a node when a release changes it: the migration.

flow.rationale: The operations and their effects first, then the hard case they reveal (splits), then the public method for that case, then the runbook that wraps it with the other consumers. The runbook's reclassification step depends on the method being explained first.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A category migration is any taxonomy change that alters which node a listing, saved search, URL, rule or metric points at, and each of six operations affects each consumer differently.

evidence.what: Rename, move, merge, split, retire and add, against listings, saved searches, URLs, fees and models, analytics and partner feeds.
evidence.shows: Only a rename leaves listings and consumers untouched; a split needs reclassification.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Merges are deterministic and splits are lossy, because a from-to mapping can name only one default target for a split, so every listing in a split category must be reclassified, which at scale is a machine-learning problem.

evidence.what: eBay's expired-category mapping returns one target per retired category, covering 'combined categories and split categories'.
evidence.shows: A public API cannot express a split as one mapping.

evidence.what: Figure 3: two boxes flow into one along single arrows; one box reaches a three-way fork where each card needs a decision.
evidence.shows: Why merges and splits differ.

transition_in.carries_over: The merge and split rows of the table.
transition_in.introduces: The difference that matters most.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Mercari reclassified more than three billion items after renewing its category structure by having a large language model label a sample and a k-nearest-neighbor classifier propagate the labels, and it published no accuracy figure.

evidence.what: GPT-3.5 Turbo for every item estimated at about USD 1 million and 1.9 years; labels for several million items chosen among about ten generated candidates; kNN over embeddings of name, description, metadata and the original category; open-source multilingual embeddings matched commercial ones; kNN 'performed satisfactorily'.
evidence.shows: A documented method for reclassification at scale, without an accuracy claim.

transition_in.carries_over: Reclassification at scale as a machine-learning problem.
transition_in.introduces: The best public case of solving it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The pattern generalizes as a large model labeling, a cheap model propagating and the old category as the strongest feature, and a live marketplace adds a confidence threshold and an audit sample that gates the run.

transition_in.introduces: The general pattern and the two safeguards a live marketplace adds.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A category migration runs as seven steps, each with a concern teams commonly forget: version the taxonomy, publish the mapping, open a dual-version window, reclassify, backfill attributes, migrate URLs and saved searches, and keep analytics comparable.

evidence.what: Figure 4: a migration as a release with a dual-version window.
evidence.shows: Consumers learn both versions before cut-over and each concern has its own step.

evidence.what: eBay's recommended-then-required pattern; Google's advice to redirect permanently 'whenever possible' and to return 404 for empty filter combinations.
evidence.source: Google Search Central, redirects (updated 2026) and faceted navigation (n.d.)
evidence.shows: The attribute and URL steps follow public guidance.

transition_in.carries_over: Reclassification with a threshold and an audit.
transition_in.introduces: The whole migration around it.

sections.heading: In Practice: The Bikes Split at Veldmark
sections.controlling_idea: Veldmark's bikes split applies the whole method: country views over one canonical Bikes node, three-tier reclassification behind an audit gate, nine other concerns migrated, and a taxonomy change that took two days of a four-week migration.

advances_thesis.how: Shows every step with numbers and the lead-time result.

transition_in.carries_over: The runbook, the reclassification pattern and the prediction rules.
transition_in.introduces: Veldmark applying them to the bikes request from the opening scene.

flow.rationale: Release, tree, listings, audit, history, everything else, elapsed time, then the program that follows. Each step uses the runbook's order, so the reader can match them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The bikes split was decided on 4 October 2027, released as version 2027.11 and effective on Monday 1 November 2027, as the first release through the taxonomy service and the first step in harmonizing the four trees.

evidence.what: Dates and release number; Figure 5: nineteen country leaves become one canonical Bikes node with seven leaves present in all four country views.
evidence.shows: The tree before and after.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Every country view enables all seven canonical leaves (the four new ones plus road, mountain, and parts and accessories) with local labels, and Polish navigation keeps bikes under its 'Sport i hobby' browse node while the classification underneath is shared.

evidence.what: Stadsfietsen, Vélos de ville, Rowery miejskie, Bicicletas de cidade; Poland's familiar browse structure.
evidence.shows: Katarzyna's condition met by a country view, not a separate tree.

transition_in.introduces: How each country sees it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 230,000 listings in road, mountain, and parts and accessories leaves mapped one to one, and the 410,000 in generic leaves went through rules, a model and sellers.

evidence.what: Rules about 189,000 (46%); model trained on 60,000 LLM-labeled, moderator-checked listings, moved above 0.92 confidence, about 205,000 (50%); seller confirmation about 16,000 (4%).
evidence.shows: The runbook's reclassification step at Veldmark's scale.

transition_in.carries_over: The tree and its country views.
transition_in.introduces: The listings that had to move.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A moderator audit found 96.8% of automatic moves correct against a 95% gate, and its errors on e-cargo bikes, fixed by a rule and an optional electric-assist attribute (an additive change cleared by taxonomy team review in two days) rather than a new leaf, teach that when two leaves claim an item, one distinction is the category and the other an attribute.

evidence.what: Audit of 3,000 moves; errors on e-cargo bikes; fix: cargo wins over electric, and an electric assist attribute on Cargo bikes.
evidence.source: Scenario ledger; the rule is local to this chapter
evidence.shows: The leaf rule from the structural choices, applied under pressure.

evidence.what: Figure 6: listings sorted by rules, a model and sellers, with an audit gate.
evidence.shows: The three tiers and the gate.

transition_in.introduces: The audit that gated them and what it found.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Femke's archived city bike keeps its old leaf and version, and the analytics mapping view reports it as a City bikes sale, so history is translated rather than rewritten.

evidence.what: The Rotterdam city bike from March, sold and archived.
evidence.shows: The version rule from listing-aggregate working after a split.

transition_in.introduces: An archived listing that did not.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Listings were only one of the things the release had to move; nine other concerns each needed their own step.

evidence.what: Saved searches (about 1.3 million rewritten), four new attributes required on create and revise from 1 March 2028, about 2,900 new landing pages, about 2,300 redirects, fees unchanged, search mappings with old IDs until 31 January 2028, an analytics mapping view, 410 professional feeds with old codes accepted until 30 April 2028, the e-bike ad segment from 1 November.
evidence.source: Scenario ledger, categories-and-taxonomies line; local details of this chapter
evidence.shows: The runbook's other steps at Veldmark.

transition_in.introduces: Everything else the split moved.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The taxonomy change took two days of a four-week migration, and the next request, a Fatbikes leaf in December 2027, took two days in total.

transition_in.introduces: Where the four weeks went and the result that measures success.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The harmonization program applies the bikes method to the rest of the tree: release 2027.10 holds 1,640 canonical leaves, each country tree becomes a view, areas are harmonized in order of value, and a country-only node must change a contract no canonical node provides.

evidence.what: 1,640 leaves in release 2027.10; vehicles, electronics, bikes and furniture first.
evidence.shows: The method scales from one split to four trees.

transition_in.carries_over: The split as the first harmonization step.
transition_in.introduces: The rest of the program.

sections.heading: Trade-offs
sections.controlling_idea: Six decisions recur in taxonomy design and change, and most turn on whether a choice changes a contract someone depends on.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the conditions under which the chapter's defaults do not hold.

transition_in.carries_over: The choices Veldmark made in the bikes split: silent model moves above a threshold, saved searches expanded to the union, the Bikes hub kept, a central taxonomy team.
transition_in.introduces: The alternatives to each choice and when each wins.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Veldmark's bikes-split choices are defaults: the table sets six recurring decisions (reclassifying a split, saved searches after a split, the old category URL, taxonomy ownership, an external taxonomy as backbone, category versus attribute) against their alternatives, and most turn on whether a choice changes a contract, such as a schema, a fee or a policy, that sellers or other systems depend on.

evidence.what: Reclassify a split, saved searches after a split, old category URL, taxonomy ownership, external taxonomy as backbone, category versus attribute: options and when to choose each.
evidence.shows: The defaults of the chapter and the conditions that reverse them.

sections.heading: Vertical Differences
sections.controlling_idea: Verticals differ in tree shape, who chooses the category and how often the tree changes, so Veldmark's verticals share the taxonomy service and release process, not the tree contents.

advances_thesis.how: Shows where external anchors replace the internal tree and what is shared across verticals.

transition_in.carries_over: Trade-offs that hold for any marketplace.
transition_in.introduces: How those trade-offs shift by vertical.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The verticals differ less in whether they need a taxonomy than in who chooses the category and how often the tree changes, which decides where the migration machinery earns its cost.

evidence.what: General classifieds, real estate, automotive and jobs by tree shape, who chooses, change cadence, external anchor, typical migration and main risk.
evidence.shows: Automotive changes monthly with a licensed taxonomy; real estate almost never; general classifieds are where splits are frequent.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: At Veldmark the verticals share the taxonomy service and release process, not the tree contents, and classifying Tradeyard Poland's cars against Motorvane's vehicle taxonomy makes their overlap measurable.

evidence.what: Motorvane maps a licensed vehicle taxonomy and releases when the provider does; Hearthly's property types follow French and Spanish practice; Tradeyard's goods tree changes most; Tradeyard Poland's cars and Motorvane Poland now share a vehicle taxonomy.
evidence.shows: Share the platform, not the contents.

transition_in.introduces: What Veldmark's three verticals share and do not.

sections.heading: Failure Modes
sections.controlling_idea: Nine recurring failures each break one part of the design: IDs in code, names as identity, deleted nodes, unmigrated saved searches, day-one requirements, unmapped partner codes, broken analytics series, models on retired nodes and a growing 'Other'.

advances_thesis.how: Shows what happens when a taxonomy is treated as content or a change is not run as a migration.

transition_in.carries_over: The design, its trade-offs and their vertical variants.
transition_in.introduces: What goes wrong without it.

flow.rationale: Identity failures first (IDs in code, names as identity, deletion), then migration failures in runbook order (saved searches, attributes, partner codes, analytics, models), then the fit signal ('Other') that starts the next release.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Category IDs hard-coded in fee and moderation rules are the root of the Category Straitjacket; rules should read the category's properties from the taxonomy service instead.
Dashboards that filter by name and URLs that resolve by slug break on the first rename, because identity is the ID and everything else is a property.

transition_in.introduces: Names and slugs misused as identity.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Deleting a node orphans listings, URLs, saved searches and analytics, so nodes are retired, never deleted.

transition_in.introduces: Identity broken by deletion.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A split without saved-search migration leaves alerts silently matching nothing, and users conclude there is no supply and leave without complaining.

transition_in.introduces: Failures of migration, starting with saved searches.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A new required field enforced on existing listings blocks routine edits and pushes sellers to delete and relist, which damages freshness and creates duplicates.

transition_in.introduces: Attributes made mandatory on day one.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A dealer feed sending a retired code fails validation and its listings go stale, so inbound mappings must outlive the dual-version window.

transition_in.introduces: Partner-facing codes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: After a split, the old category's series stops and new ones start, and without a mapping view every year-on-year report becomes wrong.

transition_in.introduces: Analytics series.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A model that uses category as a feature or is trained per category degrades silently after a migration, so model owners must be on the release's consumer list.

transition_in.introduces: Ranking and price models.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A growing 'Other' share is the earliest signal that the tree no longer fits the supply and needs a release.

transition_in.introduces: The failure that tells you a migration is due.

sections.heading: The Chief Architect's View
sections.controlling_idea: The Chief Architect runs the taxonomy as an owned product, classifies changes by blast radius, keeps releases regular, measures fitness and shares identity and contracts while presentation stays local.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the governance that makes the design last.

transition_in.introduces: The governance that prevents them.

flow.rationale: Ownership first, then how changes are classified and released, then how fitness is measured, then the principle that bounds sharing. Each needs an owner to exist.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Run the taxonomy as a product with an owner: at Veldmark a small team in Common Ground owns the canonical tree, service and releases, and brand and country managers own their views.
Classify changes by blast radius, so that cosmetic changes take the same day, additive ones two days and structural ones two to four weeks, and only cross-group changes go to the architecture forum.

evidence.what: Change class, examples, who decides and lead-time target.
evidence.shows: Not every change needs a committee.

transition_in.introduces: How the owner sorts changes.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: A monthly release train with a published calendar lets consumers plan, and emergency releases are rare and reserved for legal changes.

transition_in.introduces: The rhythm in which they ship.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five metrics measure the taxonomy's fitness: lead time for a new category, share of 'Other', correction rate, prediction acceptance and consumers on the current release.

evidence.what: Metric, what it reveals and Veldmark's direction, including lead time from six weeks (2027 baseline) to two days.
evidence.shows: The straitjacket's removal is measurable.

transition_in.introduces: How to tell whether they serve the marketplace.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The canonical tree shares identity and contracts while presentation stays local, which is the 'share platforms, not products' principle applied to reference data.

transition_in.introduces: The limit of sharing: Poland stays Polish.

sections.heading: Questions to Ask
sections.controlling_idea: Ten review questions test a platform against the chapter's design.

advances_thesis.how: Turns the design into questions the reader can ask of their own platform.

transition_in.introduces: Questions to take into a design review.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Ten questions test ownership and history, IDs in code, separate navigation, release contents, reclassification, saved searches and URLs, partner code windows, models, country trees and the 'Other' share.

conclusion.heading: From Categories to Attributes
conclusion.synthesis: The six weeks came from treating the most widely shared key as content, and stable IDs with presentation derived, releases that carry their own mapping and a migration runbook together move the cost of a change from the tree to the migration.
conclusion.so_what: Lead time for a new category is the measure to watch: once the cost sits in the migration, an additive change such as Fatbikes takes two days.

callback.to: The opening question, what a category is, and Daan's six weeks for a new leaf.
callback.how: The reader can now see 'where the listing goes' as a property of the navigation layer and the six weeks as a cost of hard-coded IDs, not of the tree.

takeaway.content: Measure lead time for a new category in your own platform and move IDs out of code; then read attribute-schemas for the schemas each category selects.

hand_off.carries_over: The category, which decides which schema applies but does not define it, and the new e-bike attributes the bikes split introduced.
hand_off.introduces: The next layer down: the attribute dictionary, the category schemas that bind it and the governance that keeps one definition true in every system.

transition_in.carries_over: The questions and the design they test.
transition_in.introduces: What the design adds up to and where the reader goes next.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The six weeks came from treating the platform's most widely shared key as content, and the chapter's design moves the cost of a category change from the tree to the migration, which is why lead time for a new category is the measure to watch.

evidence.what: Fatbikes in two days; 'where the listing goes' as a description of the navigation layer only.
evidence.shows: The design works on the opening request.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Categories decide which schema applies but do not define the schemas, which need a dictionary, types, units, enumerations and governance of their own, and attribute-schemas designs them.

evidence.what: Battery capacity for e-bikes, the energy class on every French apartment, the 31 attributes a VIN decode fills for the Essen Golf.
evidence.shows: The next layer is already in use across verticals.

transition_in.introduces: What it selects: the attribute schemas of the next chapter.
